posts.cooked: What questions do you always ask potential suppliers before placing an order?

Steady quality and on-time shipping are guaranteed among many. I think this is the biggest bottleneck in our business. It has a chain effect when one fails to deliver; as if it’s not difficult enough to maintain customer trust if this happens, we can’t keep postponing forever.

Beyond quality and shipping time I always ask what their return or damage process looks like for bulky or fragile items specifically, and get it in writing. That’s the thing that actually costs money later, not the stuff that shows up in a sample order.

One thing I’d add before placing a meaningful order is to verify the legal company behind the supplier, not just the storefront or Alibaba profile.

I’d check the Chinese legal name, registration status, registered business scope, legal representative, and whether the company named on the invoice/payment instructions matches the entity you think you’re dealing with. If those don’t line up, I’d ask for clarification before sending a deposit.

Different names don’t automatically mean fraud, but unexplained inconsistencies are worth resolving before payment.

From the other side of the counter, since I co own a print supplier (Tshirtgang, full disclosure), these are the questions the smart buyers ask us and the ones I wish more did:

Where is it actually made and shipped from. Not the head office, the facility. That decides your delivery time and your customs headaches.

What happens when something arrives wrong. Who pays for the reprint and the shipping, and how fast. Get it in writing before the first order.

Can I order one sample at the real price. If the sample costs more than the unit price, that tells you something about the real unit price.

How long have you been doing this. A supplier that has been around a few years has already made the mistakes you are worried about.

And the one almost nobody asks: what is your busiest month and what happens to turnaround then. Q4 is when suppliers fail and that is when it costs you the most.

Great list already. One angle I’d add from running a dropshipping store where products sync automatically:

Ask how their stock data works, not just how much stock they have.

How often is inventory updated? Real-time, hourly, daily? If it updates once a day, you will sell things that are already gone.

Is stock reported per warehouse? “In stock” can mean overseas when you’re promising US delivery times.

Do SKUs and variant IDs stay the same over time? If they change without notice, your listings and stock sync break silently.

What happens if an item goes out of stock after the customer already paid? Do they notify you, substitute, or just delay?

How fast is tracking uploaded after shipping? Customers start asking within 48 hours.

In my experience, most supplier problems aren’t bad products. They’re bad information. Checking this before the first order saves a lot of refunds later.

Great thread. One question I always add is asking for a small paid sample before committing to any real volume, since the sample tells you more than any catalogue claim. I also ask how they handle damaged or wrong items, including who covers the reprint and the return shipping. Clear answers on both usually tell you how reliable the supplier will be when something inevitably goes wrong.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
Before placing a supplier order, buyers recommend checking more than product quality and quoted delivery times. Reliability matters because delays or inconsistent quality can disrupt operations and damage customer trust. A paid sample at the real price can help assess the product before committing to volume.

Key checks include:
- **Problems and returns:** Get written terms for damaged, incorrect, bulky, or fragile items, including who covers replacements and return shipping and how quickly issues are resolved.
- **Supplier identity and fulfillment:** Verify the legal company behind the storefront, confirm invoice and payment details match, and establish where goods are actually made and shipped from.
- **Capacity and timing:** Ask how long the supplier has operated and how turnaround changes during its busiest season, especially Q4.
- **Inventory and tracking:** For dropshipping, clarify stock-update frequency and warehouse location, whether SKUs remain stable, how stockouts are handled, and when tracking information is uploaded.

The discussion offers a checklist rather than a single agreed standard; no supplier decision or broader resolution is reported.
